title: 50hz power filter rather than 60hz power filter
what_they_did: The definitive forum thread on 50 vs 60 Hz: there is no fixed analog mains notch in the hardware, the GUI switch is a software notch, and the ADS1299's 24-bit range and DRL tolerate 50-150 mVpp of interference before saturating.
useful_for_us: Tells us not to design a hardware 50 Hz notch for the EU recording plan; use the software notch/bandpass and matched electrode impedances, and keep the BIAS drive working.

title: Change sampling rate (frequency)
what_they_did: How to change the ADS1299 sample rate: edit the CONFIG1 low nibble in the Cyton Daisy firmware (0xB6 to 0xB4 for 1 kSPS); 16-channel Daisy defaults to 125 Hz because of the wireless bottleneck; wired USB at 460800 baud reaches 500 Hz.
useful_for_us: The exact reason Daisy's 16-channel mode is capped at 125 Hz, which is why prototype-v1 rules the Cyton+Daisy out as the main jaw-EMG recorder.

title: Prospects for higher sample rates?
what_they_did: Long throughput thread: 16 channels at 1 kHz needs about 400 kb/s, the RFduino BLE link is the bottleneck, and the proposed routes are SPI WiFi (ATWINC1500), BT 2.x modules or an isolated USB-serial connection.
useful_for_us: Sets the wireless budget for our 16-channel bench recorder and confirms that the stock OpenBCI BLE path cannot carry it; the numbers feed the nRF5340 vs ESP32 decision.

title: skin-impedance measurement of active vs. passive electrodes
what_they_did: Compares a Cognionics active dry cap with passive dry electrodes on the same ADS1299 board: the active buffer lowers the lead-off impedance reading from about 40 kOhm to 4 kOhm but the measured SNR and 50 Hz noise are nearly identical.
useful_for_us: Warns that the ADS1299 lead-off reading is misleading behind an active buffer, so we must judge the jaw-arm active pads by recorded noise, not by the GUI impedance number.

title: How to practically increase sample rate?
what_they_did: How to push the Cyton above 250 SPS: the RFduino link is bottlenecked at 115200 baud, so the practical route is the SPI WiFi shield or an external serial port with an optoisolator, with 1 kHz and 460800 baud as the targets.
useful_for_us: Quantifies the stock BLE bottleneck for the 16-channel plan and names the two workarounds (WiFi shield, isolated serial), both of which push us away from the stock Cyton link.

title: Why we need reference electrodes in bi-polar configuration
what_they_did: Explains why a bipolar EMG channel still needs the BIAS lead (to centre the differential amplifiers and cancel common mode), that SRB2/SRB1 should be off for those channels, and that the saved file reflects hardware settings, not GUI filters.
useful_for_us: Fixes our jaw/face EMG wiring: differential pair on the muscle, SRB2/SRB1 off for those channels, one BIAS on neutral tissue, and all filtering done in post-processing.

title: ADS1299 common-mode interference problem ?
what_they_did: A builder replicating the OpenBCI circuitry gets common-mode-dominated noise with SRB2 on; the thread checks the SRB1/SRB2 configuration and the requirement that VREFP minus VREFN is 0.5 V, with x24 gain on 8 channels.
useful_for_us: Adds VREF=0.5 V and an SRB1/SRB2 audit to our ADS1299 bring-up, and shows the symptom of getting it wrong: a common-mode-dominated recording that looks like bad electrodes.

title: Newbie question - OpenBCI for surface EMG / EEG of cranial nerves?
what_they_did: Covers facial EMG with Cyton vs Ganglion: the Cyton ADS1299 front end has better noise characteristics, snap electrodes are more comfortable on the face, and Cyton+Daisy samples all 16 channels at exactly the same instant.
useful_for_us: Supports snap/foam electrodes for the face and the paired 16-channel borrowed-EMG design, where all channels must be sampled simultaneously for per-channel subset scoring.

title: Sample rate of 1kHz for EMG cursor control, How?
what_they_did: One-channel facial-EMG cursor project: BLE cannot sustain >250 Hz in real time, so the user settles on 250 Hz with a 10-125 Hz bandpass because facial motor units rarely fire above 100 Hz.
useful_for_us: Direct evidence that a 250 Hz wireless jaw-EMG link is enough for a facial EMG interface, which lowers the throughput bar for our BLE pod and supports a 10-125 Hz band.

title: Help with 50 Hz noise bursts
what_they_did: Intermittent 50-60 Hz bursts with FRI dry electrodes on a Cyton; the suspects are dry electrodes in general, worn AgCl comb tips, and the WiFi shield, and the advice is to inspect/replace the tips or move to gel.
useful_for_us: Gives us a field-maintenance rule for the dry jaw pads: check tip plating and rule out the radio before re-recording a session that shows intermittent mains bursts.

title: Recording microphone / audio signals on OpenBCI for use as a trigger channel
what_they_did: How to record a mic/line signal as an OpenBCI trigger channel: attenuate with a voltage divider to <200 uV, lower the channel gain to 1x, take it off bias/SRB2, and keep the trigger cable away from the EEG/EMG leads.
useful_for_us: Gives us a safe way to add an acoustic sync track to the silent-speech recordings without railing an ADS1299 channel or inductively coupling the mic lead into the jaw EMG channels.

title: Required sampling rate for EMG
what_they_did: Answers on the sampling rate EMG needs: 250 Hz is enough for the amplitude envelope, 800 Hz-1 kHz is needed for exact waveform, the WiFi shield reaches 1000 Hz, and Cyton V3 logs to SD at up to 16 kHz.
useful_for_us: Backs the prototype decision to run the silent-speech envelope at 250-500 Hz per channel and to test 1 kHz only if waveform shape matters; it also explains why Daisy's 16-channel mode drops to 125 Hz.

title: MyoWare and EMG, need to adjust SRB, Bias?
what_they_did: Moderator answer on SRB/BIAS for MyoWare and EMG: EMG-only needs no SB adjustment; in a combined EEG/EMG setup take the EMG channels off SRB2; BIAS is ground/centring plus out-of-phase mains injection and must stay on the body.
useful_for_us: Sets the rule for the borrowed-EMG week with simultaneous EEG/EMG: keep one BIAS electrode on the body and peel the EMG channels off the SRB2 bus.

title: very high DC offset, maxes out ADC
what_they_did: Long sessions drift to a 187,500 uV DC offset that maxes the ADS1299 ADC and produces flat periods across all channels; the thread points at the reference/bias connection, mixed electrode metals and galvanic effects, and the fix of lower gain and plain gold cups with Ten20 paste.
useful_for_us: Adds a drift check to the recording plan and confirms the 'matched metal + solid BIAS' rule; it also shows the same 187,500 uV rail figure that appears at gain x24.

title: Anti Aliasing Filters for EMG application
what_they_did: Explains that the ADS1299 data rate sets the sinc-filter bandwidth, that the front-end RC filter (about 72 kHz) is for EMI, and asks whether WiFi can actually stream above 1000 Hz for face EMG.
useful_for_us: Removes an analog anti-aliasing stage from our front-end plan: rely on the ADS1299 sinc + the RC input filter, and spend the effort on verifying wireless throughput instead.

title: Myoware, measuring muscle fatigue - asking for hardware advice
what_they_did: Choosing hardware for wireless surface EMG of six muscles: the advice is to use the Cyton (MyoWare is unnecessary because it streams raw EMG), that Ganglion compression is poor for raw EMG, and that 400-500 Hz is reachable with the WiFi shield.
useful_for_us: Reinforces the decision to stream raw EMG from an ADS1299-class front end rather than a MyoWare pre-processing board, and gives the practical 400-500 Hz target.

title: Understanding the Bias pin with Myoware + ECG
what_they_did: Long thread on one bias/ground for many EMG/ECG sensors: use exactly one body bias connection, take EMG/ECG channels off the SRB and Bias busses, skip a MyoWare because Cyton already streams raw EMG, 3-4 ft leads are fine, and a flat lithium pack is preferred for wearability.
useful_for_us: Confirms our raw-ADS1299-with-simple-differential-leads choice over MyoWare boards and fixes the bias topology for a multi-channel face/jaw montage. The local extract padded its parts list; this entry uses only the parts the thread names.

title: Using the ganglion board to read EMG detecting subvocalizations for biofeedback to train suppression
what_they_did: A user wants throat EMG to train subvocalization suppression; the answer is to use foam pre-gelled Ag/AgCl button electrodes with snap connectors for sEMG rather than gold cups, and to feed back audio.
useful_for_us: Names the electrode type for throat/under-chin sEMG (pre-gelled Ag/AgCl buttons) and confirms our plan to use this region for a silent-speech signal rather than only EEG.

title: DIY Cyton Board: ADS1299 Clamping Signal
what_they_did: A DIY Cyton-firmware ADS1299 board clamps its signal because unused analog inputs were tied to AVDD; with SRB2 on, every IN*P pin is bussed to that AVDD, so the whole front end is pulled to the rail.
useful_for_us: A specific layout bug to avoid on our own ADS1299 board: never tie unused inputs to AVDD; disable unused channels in firmware and keep SRB2 only for the reference bus.

title: How steady is Cyton's sampling rate? [resolved]
what_they_did: Thread on Cyton sample-rate stability: the hardware is stable at 250/125 Hz but has no crystal, measured ~250.3 Hz with drift; erratic 111-399 Hz readings come from OS scheduling and serial buffering, and LSL/Brainflow TCP streams are steadier than OSC/GUI, with 200-300 ms marker-timing error over 10 minutes.
useful_for_us: Forces a timestamp-calibration step in the recording plan and tells us to use LSL/Brainflow rather than OSC, and not to trust the GUI's displayed rate for the silent-speech timing analysis.

title: Subvocalization Pins/Settings
what_they_did: A user recording subvocalization with paste and gold cups on the face rails the Cyton; the answers say to lower the scale/gain for EMG rather than use the EEG default, reference near the muscle, and try several ground/reference locations.
useful_for_us: Directly on our topic: expect to rail when the first subvocalization test reuses EEG gain and an EEG reference position; start at low gain and put the reference next to the muscle.

title: impedances, less with pressure; what is normal range? [resolved]
what_they_did: Thread with measured dry-electrode impedances (100-200 kOhm good, >2-3 MOhm shows RAILED) and the explanation that the ADS1299 1 GOhm input makes 1-2 MOhm acceptable (<0.1% error at 1 MOhm).
useful_for_us: Lets us stop chasing wet-electrode impedance on the hidden jaw/ear pads; 1-2 MOhm dry contact is usable, and a RAILED flag means contact or reference trouble, not 'impedance too high'.

title: noise in signal from my DIY ADS1299 board (not Cyton)
what_they_did: DIY ADS1299 board with dry FRI electrodes shows unstable high-frequency noise and discontinuities; the thread traces it to mixing gold-plated ear clips with silver-chloride dry electrodes and to grounding, and recommends consistent metals plus star-grounding.
useful_for_us: Concrete BOM rule: buy the jaw-arm reference and bias electrodes in the same metal as the signal pads, or expect galvanic offset and drift on the hidden channels.

title: EEG Cap Kit noise issue / EEG+EMG+EOG / AGND [resolved]
what_they_did: A combined EEG/EMG/EOG setup picked up heavy 50 Hz on the EMG channel while using AGND as reference; removing the AGND lead and using BIAS instead, plus switching the EMG channel off SRB/Bias, fixed it.
useful_for_us: Names a specific mistake to avoid: never use AGND as the jaw-EMG reference in a mixed montage; use the driven BIAS and keep the EMG channels off the EEG reference bus.

title: Do OpenBCI products have "international approval"?
what_they_did: Moderator answer on approval and safety: OpenBCI boards are not medical devices and need no IEC 60601 certification, the battery-powered design is the shock protection, the ADS1299 is used in certified devices, and Cyton has been compared to a certified g.tec amplifier.
useful_for_us: Supplies the safety/IRB paragraph for the borrowed-EMG and wearable plan: battery-only operation, no mains-connected amplifier on the body, and the Cyton-vs-g.tec comparison as the published precedent.

title: Sensitivity to background noise problem Ganglion vs Cython
what_they_did: Reports that a Ganglion shows large step artifacts near AC equipment where a Cyton does not; the explanation is the Ganglion AD8237 lower input impedance versus the ADS1299 1 GOhm input, and the advice is to stay off mains, run on laptop battery and avoid body ground loops.
useful_for_us: Confirms the prototype's preference for ADS1299-class front ends on dry face/jaw pads: a lower-impedance AFE turns nearby mains into large artifacts, exactly what a worn device meets.

title: ThinkPulse active electrodes, Q&A
what_they_did: Reports that ThinkPulse active dry electrodes rail the ADS1299 at the default x24 gain; the fix is to set x8 or x12 before streaming (via Brainflow config_board), and the thread debates SRB1/SRB2/BIAS ear-clip wiring for dry electrodes.
useful_for_us: Drove our gain policy: start every dry-electrode jaw channel at x8-x12, never x24, and budget a gain-setting step in the PiEEG/Brainflow bring-up before the first recording.

title: Bias Pinout
what_they_did: Answers whether BIAS_DRV and BIAS_INV are connected on the Cyton and Daisy boards: they are, so the bias amplifier has its negative feedback; the TI test diagram that shows them separate is not the normal configuration.
useful_for_us: Removes a possible false alarm when we review our own ADS1299 bias schematic, and tells us what to verify: BIAS_DRV-to-BIAS_INV continuity.

title: How do we change the sampling frequency of the WiFi board?
what_they_did: How to change the WiFi shield sample rate: set it via the GUI/SDK, the WiFi chip tops out near 1 kHz, and the thread advises separate 4xAA packs for the Cyton and the shield plus WiFi Direct and UDPx3 transfer.
useful_for_us: If the bench recorder uses the WiFi shield, budget a second battery pack and accept the ~1 kHz ceiling; do not expect the ADS1299's 16 kSPS to survive the radio.

title: Why is there no ground electrode on myoware?
what_they_did: Explains that a MyoWare board has no separate body ground because its bipolar naming is [mid, end, reference], while OpenBCI uses [electrode, reference, ground]; the two 'reference' meanings are different.
useful_for_us: Prevents a wiring mistake if any MyoWare board ends up in the borrowed-week kit: its 'reference' is a differential input, not the body ground or the SRB2 reference.

title: Once cannot start the system/session but twice
what_they_did: A custom ESP32 + ADS1299 board speaks the Cyton WiFi protocol to OpenBCI GUI 4.1.2 but fails to start streaming on GUI 5.0.4+ (BOARD_WRITE_ERROR) and shows the GUI reading CHnSET bias/SRB bits back incorrectly; no fix was posted.
useful_for_us: Tells us the cheap ESP32+ADS1299 streaming route has a real firmware/protocol risk with current OpenBCI software; if we use it, pin the GUI/driver version and verify the register readback before a recording.

title: Bias feedback
what_they_did: Thread on persistent 50 Hz on Cyton: the BIAS_DRV to BIAS_INV bridge is what enables the active DRL; without it the bias loop floats, and a higher-gain feedback loop improves 50/60 Hz rejection.
useful_for_us: Gives us a bring-up checklist item for our own ADS1299 board: verify BIAS_DRV is tied to BIAS_INV and the bias RC values match the Cyton reference design before blaming the electrodes.

title: Very strong noise in the Delta waves range
what_they_did: A builder of a 3-channel dry ADS1299 device finds strong delta-band noise traced to stainless-steel electrodes, plus mV-to-100 mV DC offset, and later WiFi-vs-Bluetooth noise; the fix is Ag/AgCl/gold/silver/tin electrodes, a 0.5 Hz high-pass and a star-grounded mixed-signal layout.
useful_for_us: Rules out steel for the jaw arm and puts the DC-offset fix (0.5 Hz high-pass, matched metal) into our electrode spec; also warns that an on-board WiFi radio raises the noise floor of the same ADS1299.

title: How far apart do ground, ref, and signal electrodes have to be?
what_they_did: Answers on spacing ground, reference and signal electrodes: do not short ground and reference, keep the active signal electrode away from ground/reference because EEG/EMG is differential, and put the bias ground on the midline so the counter-mains signal radiates evenly.
useful_for_us: Constrains the crowded geometry of the jaw-line arm: the signal pads must not sit against the REF or BIAS pad, or the channel amplitude collapses.

title: openbci-ceegrids CythonDaisy Board- GUI
what_they_did: A cEEGrid + Cyton + Daisy user loses the second 8 channels, then sees all channels jump from 100 uV to 2000 uV; the thread points at the reference electrode contact and the required Y-splitter cable between Cyton and Daisy, and at the 50/60 Hz notch setting.
useful_for_us: When we test the cEEGrid option, check the SRB2 Y-split and the reference pad first: an all-channel amplitude jump is a reference problem, not 16 separate noisy electrodes.

title: In search of old hardware schematic for the ads1299 breakout board
what_they_did: A request for an old compact ADS1299 breakout schematic; the replies point at the current PiEEG board as the better route but warn it may not follow TI star-ground/multi-plane practice and that it recommends tying the Pi digital ground to the client, and to run it battery-powered / IEC 60601-aware.
useful_for_us: This is the only substantive PiEEG discussion in the kept set. It converts our PiEEG-16 buy into a 'test the ground strategy first' item: measure the noise floor with the Pi grounded and floating before trusting it for low-amplitude jaw EMG.

title: "Verbal mind reading" using OpenBCI tech
what_they_did: A request for a device to read words from EEG/EMG: the answer is that non-invasive EEG is not accurate enough for verbal mind reading yet, and the suggestion is to look at subvocalization and facial-muscle EMG, with invasive 6-word BCIs at 79%/23% as the comparison.
useful_for_us: Independent evidence that facial EMG is the realistic silent-speech route and that even invasive word decoding is weak; useful framing for the prototype's expectations.

title: Low-frequency noise (instability?) when BIAS amp is used on custom Cyton-based board
what_they_did: Low-frequency bias-amp oscillation on a custom Cyton-based board when electrodes lose contact; the frequency changes with electrode impedance and only appears with the bias amplifier active; suspects are a floating BIASINV pin and a mistuned RC network.
useful_for_us: A failure mode to test on the dry jaw arm specifically: when contact is intermittent, the driven-bias loop can oscillate, so the pod needs contact detection or a bias network copied from the reference design.

title: Real-time speech recognition ?
what_they_did: A user asks for real-time speech decoding from an EEG headset; the moderator answers that EEG resolution is too low for detailed speech and that EMG around the mouth and jaw is the better route, and points at an OpenBCI-based commercial speller.
useful_for_us: The forum independently recommends the approach this project is built on (jaw/facial EMG for speech), which we can cite as prior-art context in the prototype note.

title: cEEGrid missing second half of channels (9–16)
what_they_did: A 16-channel cEEGrid loses channels 9-16 (flat 0 uV) after a few minutes; the cause is a weak Daisy-to-Cyton link and the missing Y-split of the L6 REF electrode to the SRB2 pin on both boards.
useful_for_us: Same failure mode as thread 3887 from the other direction: when the hidden-set test uses a cEEGrid, the SRB2 Y-split between boards is mandatory, or half the channels silently die.

title: EEG Headband Kit Compatibility with Third-Party Boards
what_they_did: Asks whether OpenBCI EEG Headband Kit electrode cables fit a third-party PiEEG IronBCI board; the answer is that they are plain 0.1 inch (2.54 mm) female headers and slide onto any header pins.
useful_for_us: Removes an adapter from the PiEEG-16 BOM: OpenBCI/standard 0.1 inch electrode cables connect directly, so the jaw-arm harness can reuse the same cables.

title: DIY EEG Headset: Does my ADS1299-based architecture make sense?
what_they_did: A DIY ADS1299 headset designer is told to drop ESP32 WiFi in favour of an nRF52840: ESP32 TX draws 150-200 mA for 20 dBm and adds EMI, while BLE5 on nRF52840 draws 5-10 mA at +4 dBm with 7.5 ms connection intervals and packet retransmission.
useful_for_us: Independent forum confirmation of the prototype's nRF53 BLE choice over ESP32 for a head-worn ADS1299 pod, with the power/EMI numbers we can reuse in the design note.

title: TTL trigger output synchronization for external electrical stimulator
what_they_did: A researcher asks whether Cyton can output a deterministic hardware TTL trigger for an external stimulator; the answer is no - use another microcontroller or timing source and capture the pulse on the Cyton aux channels.
useful_for_us: Sets our marker architecture: the sync pulse must be generated outside the ADS1299 board and recorded back on an aux/trigger channel.

title: Using cEEGrid for trigeminal / jaw reflex electrophysiology
what_they_did: The cEEGrid author answers that cEEGrid works for jaw clenching, peri-auricular EMG and trigeminal/jaw reflexes using feature engineering plus simple ML, at 1-60 Hz with Cyton+Daisy (125 Hz) or 1-125 Hz with Cyton only (250 Hz).
useful_for_us: Direct evidence that an ear-worn flex array can see jaw/peri-auricular muscle activity, which supports the Option A mastoid/behind-ear pod and gives the usable bandwidth at each channel count.

title: Open-source PRAYCG pipeline: OpenBCI/LSL media protocol, timing QC, and exploratory EEG/autonomic
what_they_did: An open-source OpenBCI/LSL/BrainFlow acquisition pipeline (PRAYCG) with LabRecorder, an ALS-PT19 light sensor for physical screen-timing validation and a Faraday enclosure; the poster's next priorities list includes a Cerelog 16-channel v2 board and Cerelog + OpenBCI EMG.
useful_for_us: The only Cerelog mention anywhere in the kept 300 threads, and it carries no Cerelog data. It tells us the forum cannot de-risk the Cerelog ESP-EEG buy, so that has to come from the vendor or a bench test.

title: Leakage-controlled baselines on 3 public imagined/silent speech datasets before building a 16-ch rig
what_they_did: A builder reports leakage-controlled baselines on three imagined/silent-speech datasets: sEMG voiced-to-silent transfers above null, EEG spoken-to-imagined does not, same-trial splits fake a transfer effect (8.7%) that temporal-block splits remove (6.4%), and electrode repeatability is the first gate.
useful_for_us: An external, current check on our own silent-speech assumptions: use temporal-block splits, expect sEMG transfer rather than EEG, and measure electrode repeatability across sessions before trusting any decoding result.
